title: Why is the trace-field guard a hardcoded list, and how is an invalid link removed?
statement: Two related defects in the typed mutation layer, both measured on 2026-09-02. FIRST: reviseArtifact blocks trace fields by testing against a hardcoded array of seventeen names, and at least nine trace fields in the current schema set are missing from it — blocks, raisedBy, satisfies, evaluates, verifies, fulfils, acceptedBy, implementedBy and answeredBy. Writes to those bypass the link operations' guards, including resolveQuestion's existence and non-dangling checks. The schemas already declare which fields are trace links through x-traceTarget, and the effective-schema resolver already reads them, so the list is a second hand-maintained model of something the schema states. SECOND: unlinkTrace validates the target type before removing, so a link that is invalid — however it got there — cannot be removed through the typed path at all. What is the right shape: derive the guard from x-traceTarget, let unlinkTrace remove unconditionally, or both?
notes: ⚠️ THE SECOND HALF IS THE ONE WITH NO WORKAROUND. A wrong-target link makes the lint block, and the operation that exists to remove links refuses to remove exactly the links that need removing. The only route today is reviseArtifact, which works solely because of the first defect — one bug is currently the escape hatch for the other. ⚠️ SEQUENCE THE FIX: `unlinkTrace` FIRST, then derive the trace-field guard from the schemas' `x-traceTarget` declarations. Doing the guard first would close the escape hatch while the links it currently repairs are still unremovable by any typed path, with hand-editing forbidden by #88 — which would leave the graph with damage the lint reports and nothing can fix. ⚠️ SCHEDULED AHEAD OF PHASE 2 GRAPH WORK, DECIDED 2026-09-03. It was previously parked behind the agent-delivery layer on the grounds that the lint catches every consequence. That is still true and is no longer sufficient: the lint detects the damage and offers no valid repair, and the defect has now been hit three times in ordinary work — a mistyped link during authoring, a routine supersession leaving a stale `answeredBy`, and a retarget where `implements` was guarded while `evaluates` was not covered by the hardcoded list at all. Phase 2 begins with far more graph editing than Phase 1 did, so the rate will rise rather than fall. ⚠️ THREE INSTANCES, EACH FROM A DIFFERENT DIRECTION: authoring error, lifecycle event, and deliberate restructuring. That spread is the argument — this is not one careless edit, it is a guard whose coverage and whose inverse operation were both derived by hand.
answer: BOTH defects are fixed, in a fixed order, and the work is scheduled ahead of Phase 2's implementation rather than behind the agent-delivery layer. FIRST `unlinkTrace` stops validating the target type on removal — validating it there refuses precisely the operations that repair an unsound graph, and it also gives `answeredBy` the removal route `resolveQuestion` cannot provide. SECOND, and only then, `reviseArtifact`'s guard is derived from the schemas' `x-traceTarget` declarations instead of a hardcoded list of seventeen names. The order matters because today one defect is the only escape hatch for the other: closing the guard first would leave invalid links unremovable by any typed path while #88 forbids hand editing. Recorded as DEC-0031, with TSK-0069 then TSK-0070, and Phase 2's entry task depends on both so the ordering lives in the graph rather than in a note.
